title: Decidability of stochastic resolvability for \(\omega\)-automata
formal: For each of the two acceptance conditions \(c\in\{\mathrm{B\ddot uchi},\mathrm{coB\ddot uchi}\}\), is stochastic resolvability decidable for finite nondeterministic word automata with condition \(c\)? More precisely, does there exist a deterministic Turing machine that, on every encoded automaton \(\mathcal A\) of that type, halts and decides whether there exists a finite-memory stochastic resolver \(\mathcal R\) such that \[\forall w\in L(\mathcal A),\qquad \Pr_{\mathcal R,w}[\text{the constructed run of }\mathcal A\text{ is accepting}]=1?\] The resolver is chosen before the word and must work for every accepted word; the word is fixed independently of its random choices. The source asks both the Büchi and coBüchi questions, and their decidability statuses are to be determined separately.

source_formulation.text: Is it decidable to check if a given (co)Büchi automaton is SR?
source_formulation.caption: Original source question; §6, p. 57:16

why: This problem asks when nondeterministic specifications can be executed online with finite memory and reliable random choices. It isolates a precise gap between deterministic resolution against an adaptive environment and probabilistic behavior on every fixed input. A decision procedure would recognize which existing automata admit such execution; an undecidability theorem would establish a limitation even for two elementary acceptance conditions on finite graphs.
status_note: Source-open in MFCS 2025 §6. The revised 31 March 2026 quantitative-resolvability paper still distinguishes this almost-sure problem as open for general infinite-word acceptance classes. A bounded later-work search on 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution for either acceptance condition. Cited proof bodies were consulted for scope, not independently formalized.

progress.text: The MFCS paper establishes the structural separation of memoryless and finite-memory stochastic resolvability. Theorem 24 gives polynomial-time safety recognition, PSPACE-complete reachability/weak recognition, and undecidability of checking a supplied Büchi or coBüchi resolver; §6 retains existence of a suitable resolver as an open question.

The revised quantitative-resolvability paper distinguishes its memoryless threshold model from probability-one resolvability and records the latter as open for the more general infinite-word acceptance classes. Its negative theorem therefore does not match the target.

The exact source definitions and the later quantitative paper were rechecked. A bounded search found no matching resolution for either Büchi or coBüchi finite-memory almost-sure recognition; this is a dated literature check, not proof that no resolution exists.

importance.reason: A foundational recognition question for online randomized automata, separating finite-memory synthesis from verification of a supplied resolver. Its relation to history determinism, probabilistic automata and good-for-MDP composition gives it significance beyond one representation.
importance.basis: Individual assessment from the MFCS 2025 definitions, comparisons and open question, checked against the revised 2026 quantitative-resolvability paper.

sentences: A finite-memory stochastic resolver selects an automaton transition using the current letter, current state and a finite memory state.
One resolver must produce an accepting run with probability one for every accepted infinite word fixed independently of its random choices.
The question asks separately whether existence of such a resolver is decidable for Büchi and coBüchi automata.
Undecidability of verifying a supplied resolver and results for memoryless thresholds below one concern different decision problems.
A resolution would determine whether reliable randomized online execution can be recognized from a finite nondeterministic specification.

definitions: An input automaton consists of finite nonempty sets \(Q\) of states and \(\Sigma\) of letters, an initial state \(q_0\), a transition relation \(\Delta\subseteq Q\times\Sigma\times Q\), and a marked transition set \(F\subseteq\Delta\). For each state and letter at least one transition is present. A run on \(w=a_0a_1\cdots\in\Sigma^\omega\) is a sequence \(q_0\xrightarrow{a_0}q_1\xrightarrow{a_1}\cdots\) using \(\Delta\). Büchi acceptance means that transitions in \(F\) occur infinitely often; coBüchi acceptance means that they occur only finitely often. Thus \(F\) is accepting in the first convention and rejecting in the second. The language \(L(\mathcal A)\) consists of words with at least one accepting run. A resolver is a tuple \((M,m_0,\mu,p)\): a finite nonempty memory set, its initial element, a deterministic memory update \(\mu:M\times\Delta\to M\), and for each \((m,q,a)\) a probability distribution \(p_{m,q,a}\) on the outgoing transitions \(\Delta_{q,a}\). Its probabilities are arbitrary real numbers in \([0,1]\) summing to one; some may be zero. At step \(i\), the resolver observes \(m_i,q_i,a_i\), samples \(\delta_i\) with distribution \(p_{m_i,q_i,a_i}\), follows that transition and sets \(m_{i+1}=\mu(m_i,\delta_i)\). For a fixed word, finite-run cylinder probabilities are the products of these step probabilities; their induced measure on infinite runs defines the displayed probability. The memory size is finite but has no prescribed bound and may depend on the input automaton. Neither the resolver nor its probabilities are part of the finite input. Requiring rational probabilities, a fixed memory bound or memorylessness would be an additional restriction, not imposed here. The automaton and its marked transitions are explicitly listed using binary indices and delimiters; the alphabet is part of the input. Decidability means one effective machine for all such finite descriptions of the specified acceptance type, with exact yes/no output and no running-time bound. The source uses complete automata; missing transitions may equivalently lead to a fresh rejecting sink.
answer_criterion: Give Lean-checked decidability or undecidability proofs for each of the Büchi and coBüchi input classes. A decidability proof must supply an effective total algorithm and establish its correctness for the existential finite-memory, real-probability resolver semantics above. An undecidability proof must exclude every total computable decider for that class. A result for only one acceptance class settles only that component of the source question. Checking an already specified resolver, restricting its memory to one state, or replacing probability one by a smaller threshold does not settle either full existence question.

context_blocks.text: A nondeterministic automaton may accept a word because one successful run exists, even if choosing that run requires knowledge of future letters. A resolver must commit to each transition when the current letter arrives. Stochastic resolvability allows these commitments to be random while requiring failure probability zero on every accepted word.

The order of choices matters. The same resolver is used on every word, but a word cannot react to the random transitions actually taken. Requiring success against an environment that sees those transitions is the stronger adversarial notion studied alongside stochastic resolvability. Probability one here is a separate assertion for each fixed word; it does not require one common set of random choices that succeeds simultaneously on all words.

Finite memory is part of the source definition, not a consequence silently assumed in this card. Memoryless resolvers are a strictly weaker class for Büchi and coBüchi automata. The source also leaves open whether the particular nonzero probability values can always be changed while preserving success, so the definition cannot be replaced by an unproved finite search over transition supports.

The source proves that checking a supplied finite-memory resolver is undecidable for both acceptance conditions. This concerns a pair consisting of an automaton and a prescribed resolver; the present input is just an automaton and asks whether any suitable resolver exists. A failed prescribed resolver may coexist with a successful alternative, which explains why the checking theorem is not already the requested negative answer.

Related positive results help locate the boundary. Recognition is polynomial-time for safety automata and PSPACE-complete for reachability and weak automata. A safety condition rejects as soon as a bad transition occurs; reachability requires eventually entering an accepting region, and weak automata do not mix accepting and rejecting recurrence within one strongly connected component. The unrestricted Büchi and coBüchi conditions allow behaviors beyond these subclasses.

The later quantitative paper studies memoryless resolvers with a fixed success threshold strictly below one. Its undecidability theorem is explicitly separate from almost-sure stochastic resolvability with finite memory. Treating the common word “resolvability” as identifying the two problems would incorrectly retire this card.
